claim_verdicts.evidence: gitglossary, "commit object": "An object which contains the information about a particular revision, such as parents, committer, author, date and the tree object which corresponds to the top directory of the stored revision." git-commit DESCRIPTION: "Create a new commit containing the current contents of the index and the given log message describing the changes." The tree names the top directory of a stored revision — a whole state, not the differing lines.

git-cat-file: "-p  Pretty-print the contents of <object> based on its type." The field list is git-commit-tree, Commit Information: "A commit encapsulates: all parent object ids; author name, email and date; committer name and email and the commit time." The order is settled by the captured run: outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/inspect-commit.txt prints tree / parent / author … / committer … / blank / "Add a README", exactly the order the claim gives.

git-log DESCRIPTION: "List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s)". gitglossary, "parent": "A commit object contains a (possibly empty) list of the logical predecessor(s) in the line of development, i.e. its parents." The "possibly empty" case is the stop condition the claim names.

gitglossary, "DAG": "Directed acyclic graph. The commit objects form a directed acyclic graph, because they have parents (directed), and the graph of commit objects is acyclic". gitglossary, "parent": a commit holds a "list of the logical predecessor(s)" — plural, so more than one parent is allowed.

git-commit DESCRIPTION: "Create a new commit containing the current contents of the index" — the index, not the disk. git-add DESCRIPTION: "It only adds the content of the specified file(s) at the time the add command is run". gitglossary, "working tree": "The tree of actual checked out files."; "index": "A collection of files with stat information, whose contents are stored as objects."

git-status, Short Format: "X shows the status of the index and Y shows the status of the working tree", with M = modified and a space = unmodified. So " M" is modified in the work tree only and "M " is modified in the index. The captured run agrees: outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/inspect-commit.txt ends " M prices.txt" then, after git add, "M  prices.txt". (git-scm.com serves the current Git manual; this short-format rule long predates the pinned 2.46.)

git-add DESCRIPTION: "It only adds the content of the specified file(s) at the time the add command is run; if you want subsequent changes included in the next commit, then you must run git add again to add the new content to the index." Combined with git-status "X shows the status of the index and Y shows the status of the working tree", a later edit necessarily marks both columns.

git-hash-object DESCRIPTION: "Computes the object ID value for an object with specified type with the contents of the named file" — the id is a function of the contents. git-commit-tree, Commit Information: a commit encapsulates "all parent object ids", "author name, email and date", "committer name and email and the commit time" (plus the tree and the log message), so each of those fields is inside the hashed content.

git-commit --amend: "Replace the tip of the current branch by creating a new commit." git-gc DESCRIPTION: housekeeping includes "removing unreachable objects which may have been created from prior invocations of git add"; gc.pruneExpire: "When git gc is run, it will call prune --expire 2.weeks.ago". So the replaced commit survives, unreferenced, until gc prunes it.

git-commit, Commit Information: "Author and committer information is taken from the following environment variables, if set: GIT_AUTHOR_NAME, GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL, GIT_AUTHOR_DATE, GIT_COMMITTER_NAME, GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL, GIT_COMMITTER_DATE", and these "override user.name and user.email". With claim 8 (id = hash of that content) the six ids follow. Unstated conditions: the default SHA-1 object format, and identical file content and modes — which hold because both scripts re-exec inside the lab box (lab-run.sh).

git-commit DESCRIPTION: "Create a new commit containing the current contents of the index and the given log message describing the changes." — no remote, no network. git-push DESCRIPTION: "Updates one or more branches, tags, or other references in one or more remote repositories from your local repository, and sends all necessary data that isn't already on the remote."

git-add, -A/--all: "Update the index not only where the working tree has a file matching <pathspec> but also where the index already has an entry. This adds, modifies, and removes index entries to match the working tree." and "If no <pathspec> is given when -A option is used, all files in the entire working tree are updated". git-commit: "-m <msg>, --message=<msg>: Use <msg> as the commit message." — the message is supplied, so no editor is opened.

Count and ids hold: outputs/stage-0/git-playground/build-history.txt says "built /tmp/git-playground with 6 commits on main" and inspect-commit.txt lists 57a2d53, c812dbd, b3472f6, 09c8526, d915e63, 9f3b296. "each naming exactly one parent" does not hold: build-history.sh does rm -rf / mkdir / cd, then `git init --quiet --initial-branch=main`, then the first save, so 9f3b296 is a root commit. git-init: "An initial branch without any commits will be created"; gitglossary parent: a "(possibly empty) list".
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: At stage-0 the playground built by git-playground/build-history.sh has six commits on its main line of history: the oldest, 9f3b296 'Add the price list', is a root commit with no parent, and the other five name exactly one; the three newest are 57a2d53 'Add a README', c812dbd 'Explain the rounding' and b3472f6 'Round the total down to millions'.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Captured run, outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/inspect-commit.txt: under "the commit object itself:" the line "parent c812dbd1cc33d3b7b673ab3665b9e032375e5f99", and in the log listing above it "* c812dbd Explain the rounding" as the second * line. The first seven characters match, and git-log --oneline is "a shorthand for --pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit", which is where the abbreviation comes from.

scripts/git/inspect-commit.sh lines 24-27: printf of three products into prices.txt, git status --short, git add prices.txt, git status --short; the script contains no git commit at all. Captured output ends " M prices.txt" then "M  prices.txt". Note on method: `git show stage-0:<file>` and tools/extract-code were refused by this sandbox, so both code blocks were compared line by line against the checked-out examples/don-hang working tree; they match character for character.

git-log: "--oneline  This is a shorthand for --pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit used together."; "-<number>, -n <number>: Limit the output to the first <number> commits that would be shown."; "--graph  Draw a text-based graphical representation of the commit history on the left hand side of the output. This may cause extra lines to be printed in between commits, in order for the graph history to be drawn properly." The captured run shows six "* <abbrev> <message>" lines.

git-init DESCRIPTION: "This command creates an empty Git repository - basically a .git directory with subdirectories for objects, refs/heads, refs/tags, and template files." git-commit, Commit Information: the GIT_AUTHOR_* / GIT_COMMITTER_* variables are used "if set" and "override user.name and user.email". build-history.sh exports all four names above its git config lines and save exports both dates, so the config values are the fallback only.

gitglossary, "working tree": "The tree of actual checked out files. The working tree normally contains the contents of the HEAD commit's tree, plus any local changes that you have made but not yet committed." The glossary carries no "working directory" entry, so naming "working tree" as Git's own term is right.

Declared an opinion in the ledger, and outline item 4 in content/tracks/foundation/track.yaml makes it the lesson's contract: "git status and git log --oneline --graph are the two commands to run before anything else, every time." The lesson states it as "a habit worth keeping", i.e. with a hedge, so no documentation sentence is being asserted and none can settle it.

gitformat-pack: "However to save space, an object could be stored as a 'delta' of another 'base' object." and pack entries hold "compressed delta data" / "deflated bytes". So delta and compression are a storage detail while the commit still names a whole tree (claim 1). git-show DESCRIPTION: "For commits it shows the log message and textual diff" — the difference is produced when asked for.

scripts/git/inspect-commit.sh line 7 is "/repo/git-playground/build-history.sh >/dev/null", before "cd /tmp/git-playground" and every read command; build-history.sh line 9 is "rm -rf \"$repo\" \"$origin\"", so re-running rebuilds from scratch. Line 5 of both scripts re-execs scripts/lab-run.sh, whose last line is "exec docker compose exec -T lab bash -c …" — which is why Try it step 1 still needs scripts/up.sh.

git-show DESCRIPTION: "For commits it shows the log message and textual diff." and "Some options that git log command understands can be used to control how the changes the commit introduces are shown"; the DIFF FORMATTING section lists "--stat  Generate a diffstat". Captured run: "57a2d53 Add a README", then "README.md | 14 ++++++++++++++" and "1 file changed, 14 insertions(+)".

git-commit-tree: a commit encapsulates "author name, email and date" and "committer name and email and the commit time"; git-commit takes both from the same user.name/user.email unless overridden, hence "usually the same person". gitglossary, HEAD: "The current branch. … HEAD is a reference to one of the heads in your repository, except when using a detached HEAD, in which case it directly references an arbitrary commit." git-commit: "The new commit is a direct child of HEAD".

git-status, Short Format: when -b is used "the short-format status is preceded by a line ## <branchname> <tracking-info>". The script runs exactly that form (scripts/git/inspect-commit.sh line 11: `git status --short --branch`) and the captured run begins "## main...origin/main".

issues.quote: Every commit in this playground names one parent, so what you see is a line; the graph appears as soon as a commit names two.
issues.text: False of this playground, and it contradicts the sentence two before it ("follows parents until a commit has none left"). build-history.sh empties the folder, runs `git init --quiet --initial-branch=main`, then the first `save`, so the oldest of the six — 9f3b296 'Add the price list', the last `*` line of the listing the reader is told to read — has no parent line at all. git-init: "An initial branch without any commits will be created"; gitglossary parent: a "(possibly empty) list". Claim 13 repeats the error.
issues.fix: Write "Every commit in this playground names at most one parent — the oldest, `Add the price list`, names none, which is where the walk stops — so what you see is a line; the graph appears as soon as a commit names two." Correct claim 13 in .meta.json the same way: five of the six name one parent, the root names none.

issues.quote: It sets six environment variables … Read those six lines and the two commands inside `save`
issues.text: Six variables, five lines. In the quoted block GIT_AUTHOR_NAME, GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL, GIT_COMMITTER_NAME and GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL take one line each, while GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE are set together on the single line inside `save` (`export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="$1" GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="$1"`). A reader who counts lines to find "those six lines" finds five, and the fifth is inside `save`, next to the two commands named right after.
issues.fix: Write "Read those five `export` lines and the two commands inside `save`", or "Read the four names it exports at the top and the line inside `save` that exports the two dates".

issues.quote: run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph` before anything else … In their output the line beginning `##` is about names and a copy on a server
issues.text: "Their" points at plain `git status`, which never prints a `##` line: git-status prints that line only with -b/--branch, "the short-format status is preceded by a line ## <branchname> <tracking-info>". The `##` line the reader actually sees comes from the script's `git status --short --branch`. Separately, "a copy on a server" is not what the reader will find here: build-history.sh clones the playground into a local bare directory, `${repo}-origin`.
issues.fix: Write "In the script's `git status --short --branch` output the line beginning `##` is about names and a copy kept elsewhere; ignore it and meet it in [[foundation.l2.git-branches]]."

issues.quote: `git cat-file -p HEAD` prints one commit exactly as Git stored it
issues.text: Overstated, and it collides with the lesson's own section 6 ("Git … compresses what it stores"). git-cat-file says only "-p  Pretty-print the contents of <object> based on its type"; what is on disk is a zlib-compressed object behind a type-and-length header, or a delta inside a pack (gitformat-pack: "an object could be stored as a 'delta' of another 'base' object"). The listing is the commit's content, not its stored bytes.
issues.fix: Write "`git cat-file -p HEAD` prints the content of one commit as Git recorded it — here the newest." and leave the sentence about compression in section 6 to cover storage.

issues.quote: the id of the commit you were standing on — the newest one in the history you are reading, which Git calls `HEAD`
issues.text: The gloss states as general what is only true here. gitglossary: "HEAD … is a reference to one of the heads in your repository, except when using a detached HEAD, in which case it directly references an arbitrary commit" — HEAD is the commit that is checked out, which need not be the newest in that history. Claim 23 states it correctly ("the commit currently checked out"); the lesson's wording is the one that will have to be unlearned in [[foundation.l2.git-history-and-recovery]].
issues.fix: Write "the id of the commit you are standing on, which Git calls `HEAD` — in this playground the newest one on the line of history you are reading".

issues.quote: six saved states of a tiny project: a price list and a script that totals it
issues.text: The project is described as two files, but the six commits the reader is about to inspect add four: prices.txt, total.sh, test.sh and README.md (build-history.sh lines 30-86). It matters two sections later, where the newest commit's `git show --stat` names README.md and the lesson says "`git show --stat` names the one file that commit changed" — a file the reader was told the project does not contain.
issues.fix: Write "six saved states of a tiny project: a price list, a script that totals it, a check for that script and a README" — or drop the file list and write "six saved states of a tiny project built around a price list".

issues.quote: Read those six lines and the two commands inside `save`; the rest only writes files and calls `save`:
issues.text: I went to count six lines and found four `export` lines at the top of the block. The two remaining variables, GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE, share one line inside `save` — which the same sentence treats as a separate place ("and the two commands inside `save`"). So "those six lines" points at something I cannot find, and I stopped to check whether I was looking at the right block before I could read on.
issues.fix: Replace "Read those six lines and the two commands inside `save`" with "Read the four `export` lines at the top, the line inside `save` that exports the two dates, and the two commands under it".

issues.text: The prerequisite taught me that a shell reads a line and runs the program its first word names. Nothing has said a script can make a command of its own, so `save() { … }`, `"$1"` and `"$2"` are three new things at once: I could not tell whether `save` is a git command, what `$1` stands for, or when the lines inside the braces run. The section's whole argument is that `save` fixes the dates and makes each commit, so I had to guess through its main step.
issues.fix: Add one sentence just before the block: "`save` is a command the script makes for itself; when the script later writes `save <date> <message>`, `$1` is that date and `$2` that message."

issues.quote: The first two arrows are steps you run; the last three are parent pointers, so time runs the other way and the commit furthest right is the oldest.
issues.text: The situation told me the playground holds six saved states; the diagram draws four commits and this sentence calls the rightmost one the oldest. Two paragraphs later I read that Git "follows parents until a commit has none left", so I took the rightmost node to be where the parents stop — i.e. that the playground has four commits. I could not reconcile the two counts, and the listing later shows six `*` lines, which made it worse.
issues.fix: Replace "the commit furthest right is the oldest" with "the commit furthest right is the oldest of the four drawn — the playground has two more behind it".

issues.quote: Because one commit can name two parents, and two commits can name the same parent, the shape is a graph rather than a line
issues.text: This is the sentence the title rests on, and it is the only place a graph is argued for. Both halves are asserted and neither is shown: the diagram is a line, the listing is a line, every commit in the playground has one parent, and the reason it could be otherwise is handed to a lesson I have not read. I finish able to repeat the word "graph" without being able to picture the shape the title says I should leave with.
issues.fix: After "two commits can name the same parent", add one clause the reader can picture with what they already have: "— which is what happens when two people both save starting from the same commit: two commits then name it, and the single line splits in two".

issues.quote: You expected saving to Git to be one step, the way saving a document is.
issues.text: Nothing I have read says what Git is. The prerequisite only mentioned "Git Bash" as a place where the same shell commands work. I can follow the lesson because everything it does with Git is explained step by step, but the opening asks me to already have an expectation about a program nobody has introduced.
issues.fix: Name it once in the first sentence of the situation: "you run `git-playground/build-history.sh`, which uses `git` — the program that keeps saved states of a project — to build a throwaway repository …".

issues.quote: the shape is a graph rather than a line
issues.text: "graph" is the word in the title and I only know it from charts. The sentence tells me what the shape is not (a line) but never what a graph is, so I cannot check my picture against anything.
issues.fix: Gloss it in the same sentence: "the shape is a graph — points joined by arrows, where several arrows can meet at one point — rather than a line".

issues.quote: Below it `git init` creates the empty repository, and `git config` records the same two names in the repository itself
issues.text: The prose sends me to that line, and the line reads `git init --quiet --initial-branch=main`. "branch" and "main" are words I have not met. The lesson is careful to postpone the `##` line to another lesson but says nothing about this flag, so I did not know whether I was allowed to skip it as well, or whether it was part of what makes the ids identical.
issues.fix: Extend the existing deferral at the end of the section: "the line beginning `##`, and the `--initial-branch=main` in `git init`, are about names and a copy on a server; ignore both and meet them in [[foundation.l2.git-branches]]."

issues.quote:
the two commands to run before anything else:
...
* 57a2d53 Add a README
issues.text: A line that is only `...` sits directly above the two `*` lines. I cannot tell whether the script prints it or whether it stands for output that was cut, so I cannot be sure `* 57a2d53` is really the first `*` line — and Try it asks me to count to the second one. I could only do the exercise because the prose names `c812dbd` for me a paragraph later.
issues.fix: Say what the elisions are where the block is introduced: add "the `...` lines stand for output left out here; the log prints the six commits newest first, one `*` line each."

issues.quote: Those four names, and the two dates `save` exports before every pair of commands, are not tidiness
issues.text: Section 5 holds two code blocks, an output block and five paragraphs: why the ids are fixed, author versus committer, the two steps inside `save`, `git init` and `git config`, the `cat-file` listing, why a commit cannot be edited, and a habit to keep. By the fourth paragraph I had lost the thread about ids and went back to the top of the section.
issues.fix: Move the last paragraph (the `git status` / `git log` habit) to the end of Try it, so the section ends on the `cat-file` listing it builds up to.

issues.quote: But neither is stored inside the commit object, and `git cat-file -p HEAD` never prints an address.
issues.text: "the commit object" is a term the lesson never uses — it says "one commit exactly as Git stored it". Reading the explanation I stopped to wonder whether an object is something other than a commit, which is a new question raised by the answer key rather than settled by it.
issues.fix: In q1's explanation for option c, write "inside the commit" instead of "inside the commit object" (Vietnamese: "trong commit" instead of "trong object commit").

issues.quote: True, because Git sends the snapshot away first and then keeps a copy in `.git` so that you can read it offline.
issues.text: The statement says no network is used, and this option answers "True" while describing a network being used. I ruled it out because it contradicts itself, not because of anything the lesson taught me — so the question got easier without testing whether I understood where a commit is written.
issues.fix: Give option b a verdict that matches its reason: "False, because Git sends the snapshot to the server first and keeps a copy in `.git` only so that you can read it offline."

graph (the word in the title, defined only by contrast with "a line")
branch / main / `--initial-branch=main` (the `##` line is postponed on purpose, this flag is not)
`save() { … }`, `$1`, `$2` — a command a script defines for itself
commit object (quiz q1's explanation only; the lesson says "one commit")

"save() {" with `"$1"` — nothing says a script can define its own command, or what `$1` is.
"the commit furthest right is the oldest" — but the playground was said to hold six saved states and the diagram draws four.

The `...` lines in the output block — printed, or cut out? It decides how I count `*` lines in Try it.
